title: Short is enough (Berakhot 34a)
hookLine: the Talmud points to Moses' five-word prayer: a short prayer is fine

lines: ONE STUDENT GOES ON AND ON.
cards: A study hall, long ago. A student is leading the prayer, and he goes on. And on.
Every line stretched, every word drawn out. The other students shift on their benches and finally complain to their teacher, Rabbi Eliezer. How long is this going to take?
Another day, a different student leads, and he races through it, done almost before he's started. The students complain again. Too short!
Rabbi Eliezer has one answer for both, and both answers point to Moses.

teach.b: The story is in the Talmud, Berakhot 34a. To the complainers about the long prayer, Rabbi Eliezer says: is he taking longer than Moses?
Moses lay on his face before God for forty days and forty nights, pleading for the people after the golden calf. To the complainers about the short prayer, he says: is he any shorter than Moses?
And he quotes the moment in the book of Numbers when Moses' sister Miriam is struck with a skin disease. Moses cries out: "Heal her now, O God, I beseech Thee."
In Hebrew it's five short words: El na, refa na lah. God, please, heal, please, her. That's the whole prayer.
No opening praise, no long explanation. Two pleases and a name. And it's enough.
After seven days outside the camp, Miriam is brought back in. The lesson Rabbi Eliezer draws isn't that short is better or long is better.
It's that both are real prayer. There's a time for forty days on your face, and a time for five words cried out in a hallway. The length doesn't make it count.

That's the week's last word on personal prayer, and it ties the week together. We started with the tkhine, prayer at the kitchen stove. Then Rebbe Nachman's own words, koved rosh, the dry days, the prayer of the road.
Long or short, fixed or free, Hebrew or Yiddish: the tradition makes room for all of it.

how: Many Jews add a brief personal prayer for the sick, often naming the person, in the Amidah's blessing for healing or at the Mi Sheberach when the Torah is read; Moses' words for Miriam are often cited as a model.

o: Moses' sister, healed after a five-word prayer
Moses' mother, who hid him by the river
Moses' wife, who saved him on the road to Egypt

games.q: inside the short prayer — tap the pairs.

s: the Talmud says short prayers are better than long ones
Rabbi Eliezer defends both: Moses prayed forty days, and Moses prayed five words.
Moses' prayer for Miriam is five words in Hebrew
Moses prayed for his sister Miriam
in the book of Numbers, when she is struck with a skin disease.

games.q: you're Rabbi Eliezer. your students complain the prayer leader was far too quick. what do you say?
o: he must repeat it more slowly.
is he any shorter than Moses?
games.why: he points to Moses' five words for Miriam: a short prayer is still a whole prayer.

practice: Think of one person who's struggling right now, ill, worried, grieving, and picture their face.
If you pray, borrow Moses' shape: their name, please, and the one thing they need, five words or fewer; if you don't, make it a five-word wish, and then just sit with their face.

wordCard.voice: Miriam, Moses' sister, healed after his five-word prayer, God, please, heal her, please, which the Talmud holds up as proof a brief prayer is real prayer.

orig.note: Hebrew: God, please, heal her, please (Numbers 12:13).

carryVoice: Your line: both are real prayer. A week of rain and dew, the kitchen tkhine, your own words, koved rosh, the heart that follows, safe on the way. Another week, done.

sources.q: Heal her now, O God, I beseech Thee.
